analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and natural gas by carbon content, rebating revenue through tax cuts and quarterly checks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the House and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge companies $25 for every ton of carbon dioxide emitted from the coal, oil, and natural gas they produce or import, with the fee rising $10 each year. The money would go into a fund used first to cut individual income tax rates, then for worker transition aid (especially coal communities), energy research, and infrastructure — with whatever is left paid out as quarterly cash dividends to individuals. The tax would drop to zero in any year emissions hit a set reduction target, and imports from countries without similar carbon policies would face an equivalent fee to protect U.S. producers.
analysis.who_benefits: Most households would come out ahead: the revenue funds a cut in the lowest individual income tax rates and quarterly dividend checks to anyone lawfully present with a valid Social Security number. Coal workers and coal communities would get targeted transition assistance. Cleaner air and slower climate change would benefit everyone, and U.S. manufacturers would be protected by fees on imports from countries without equivalent carbon pricing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the lowest individual income tax rates — for example the 10% bracket becomes 9% and the 12% bracket becomes 11% — paid for out of carbon tax revenue.

After funding the tax cut and transition programs, remaining revenue is paid out as quarterly dividends to every eligible individual with a valid Social Security number who is lawfully present in the United States.

20% of revenue after the tax cut goes to worker transition assistance with an emphasis on coal workers and coal communities, plus rural energy assistance, research, grid improvements, and climate-resilience projects.
The tax automatically drops to zero if emissions fall enough to hit the bill's reduction benchmarks — 30% below 2005 levels by 2025, 40% by 2030, and so on up to 80% by 2050.
An excise tax on carbon dioxide content is designed to make cleaner energy relatively cheaper, reducing emissions from the largest U.S. sources.

analysis.who_pays: Producers, miners, and importers of coal, oil, and natural gas would pay the tax, which they would pass through to consumers in higher prices for fuel, electricity, and goods made with fossil energy. Exported fuels are exempt or refundable. Industries would also face new compliance costs and a carbon equivalency fee regime at the border.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: A carbon tax raises energy prices for everyone; the offsets only partially protect households, since the income tax rate cut is modest and the quarterly rebate is limited to individuals with valid Social Security numbers who are lawfully present, excluding others who still face higher energy costs.

Starting in 2029, the per-person dividend is capped by reference to the average amount available in 2028, even though the tax rate keeps rising $10 per ton each year — meaning more revenue would flow to other uses rather than to rebate checks.
The carbon equivalency fee on imports requires complex calculations of what domestic producers incur, which could invite disputes and administrative burden for importers and customs enforcement.
Fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive industries argued such taxes threaten jobs and raise costs, which is the standard good-faith objection to carbon pricing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design follows the 'carbon fee and dividend' model: most revenue returns to households through lower tax rates and quarterly checks, and coal communities get dedicated transition money, which softens the regressive edge of energy price increases. The main unresolved problems are that the rebate pool shrinks relative to the growing tax after 2028, eligibility excludes some people who bear the higher prices, and energy-intensive industries face real cost pressure. On balance the bill was written to favor ordinary households, but its actual effect on energy prices would have been real and immediate while the benefits would have taken time to arrive.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on September 27, 2018, near the end of the 115th Congress.

It was referred to five committees — Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, Science, Space, and Technology, and Transportation and Infrastructure — for consideration of the parts under each committee's jurisdiction.
No committee held a hearing or markup, no cosponsors signed on, and the bill's only actions were its introduction and referral.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and anyone who benefits from the status quo of untaxed carbon emissions are better off, since the tax was never enacted. No one paid a price for stopping it — the bill simply never attracted enough support to move.

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his proposal to tax fossil fuels and rebate the revenue to households.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the roughly three months it had it before the Congress ended.

against.name: The other four referred committees (Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, Science, Space, and Technology, Transportation and Infrastructure)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions assigned to them.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a lone Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so it never developed a partisan profile in the record.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: They would pay $25 per ton of carbon dioxide content at the wellhead, mine, or border, rising $10 a year, and pass most of that cost to their customers. The tax is designed to shrink their market over time, though exports are exempt and their coal-employee communities would get transition funding.

U.S.-based manufacturers would be protected from foreign competitors who don't pay a carbon tax, because imports of goods made with fossil energy face an equivalent fee. But importers themselves bear new fee and compliance costs.

The bill funds technology-neutral energy research, rural energy assistance, grid improvements, and efficiency programs, and a rising carbon price makes renewable and efficiency alternatives relatively cheaper.
